articles.title: Nine Tips for Greening a Home Renovation Project
articles.summary:
Renovating a home is a great opportunity to make a home more functional, improve comfort,...
The post Nine Tips for Greening a Home Renovation Project appeared first on Earth911.
articles.content:
Renovating a home is a great opportunity to make a home more functional, improve comfort, and revitalize drab spaces. It is also a chance to keep a remarkable amount of material out of the ground.

The EPA estimates the United States generated 600 million tons of construction and demolition debris in 2018 — more than twice the volume of municipal solid waste that year — and demolition accounts for more than 90 percent of it. About 145 million tons of that went straight to landfills.

A green approach to contracting and choosing materials helps trim that waste stream and makes your home more water- and energy-efficient. One thing has changed since this article first ran: the federal tax credit that used to subsidize efficiency upgrades expired at the end of 2025, so the money math on some of these decisions now runs through state and utility programs instead. More on that below.

Apply these green tips during the planning phase of your home renovation project, whether you do the work yourself or hire a contractor.

Repurpose When Possible

Begin by exploring what existing materials and fixtures can be repurposed, donated, and recycled before sending them to a landfill.

Cabinetry, lighting fixtures, flooring, and plumbing fixtures can sometimes be refinished and repaired for a new look. Consider replacing inefficient appliances and plumbing fixtures to save money and resources in the long run instead of replacing cabinets and counters.

Donate Unneeded Materials

You can donate items that are still in good condition but don’t suit the needs of your project. The Habitat for Humanity ReStore network accepts a variety of appliances, building materials, furniture, and more, and its donation guide explains what individual stores will and won’t take.

Replace Inefficient Toilets & Appliances

Toilets are the single largest use of water inside most homes. A WaterSense labeled toilet uses no more than 1.28 gallons per flush, 20 percent below the federal standard of 1.6 gpf, and the EPA estimates the average family saves close to 13,000 gallons and more than $170 a year by replacing old, inefficient models. Older toilets can use as much as six gallons per flush.

One detail worth knowing if you are shopping for a dual-flush model: the EPA changed the specification in 2025. The full-flush mode itself must now come in at 1.28 gpf or less, rather than averaging a big flush against two small ones. Some dual-flush toilets that carried the label a few years ago no longer qualify.

The same efficiency logic applies to washers and dishwashers. When deciding whether to replace an appliance, compare its water and energy consumption to new models before you commit. A recently manufactured dishwasher, for example, may use half the energy of one installed 20 years ago.

Find Salvaged Materials

Home renovation projects that use salvaged materials can have unique character and charm. When shopping for new materials, explore where you might use reclaimed items instead. Look on Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, your local Buy Nothing group, the ReStore, or a salvage yard. Active demolition sites are worth a visit, too; contractors will often part with trim, brick, or fixtures rather than pay to haul them away.

Use Natural Finishes & Products

Many paints, varnishes, stains, and flooring materials release volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that degrade indoor air quality, and concentrations indoors routinely run higher than outdoors. Whenever possible, select finishes labeled low- or zero-VOC and look for products certified to a Green Seal standard. Ventilate well during and after application regardless of the label.

Look for Certified Green Products

Use Forest Stewardship Council-certified wood products to confirm that lumber, plywood, and flooring came from responsibly managed forests. Look for ENERGY STAR appliances, which meet more stringent energy-efficiency requirements than the federal minimum.

ENERGY STAR itself had an eventful year. The administration proposed eliminating the program in 2025; Congress instead appropriated $33 million for it in the fiscal 2026 spending package. In March 2026, EPA and the Department of Energy signed an agreement making DOE the lead agency that manages the program. The label remains a useful way to assess products even if where its specifications and staffing will be located is still unsettled.

For a broader view of what makes a building material defensible, the U.S. Green Building Council’s LEED v5 rating system, which was ratified in April 2025 and open for certification since that November, organizes its materials credits around embodied carbon and ingredient disclosure. Homeowners can’t realistically chase LEED points on a bathroom remodel, but two of the product labels it recognizes are easy to check on a spec sheet: Cradle to Cradle Certified and Declare, which functions as a nutrition label for building products.

Reduce Construction Waste & Debris

Using salvaged materials for your renovation project typically generates less packaging waste. It also feeds a recovery stream that already works better than most people assume: of the 600 million tons of construction and demolition debris generated in 2018, roughly 455 million tons were directed to a next use rather than disposal, mostly as aggregate material.

The materials that often are landfilled are the ones worth planning around. Wood, gypsum drywall, asphalt shingles, and brick and clay tile all end up in landfills at high rates, so ordering carefully and finding a home for the leftovers makes more difference than it does with concrete or metal.

When purchasing new materials, look for items with as little non-recyclable packaging as possible. Consider donating surplus materials or finding new ways to make good use of them when your renovation is complete, and check Earth911’s recycling search for local options before anything goes in a dumpster.

Make Energy-Saving Improvements

Is your home properly insulated and air sealed? Are there rooms with drafts or uneven temperatures? A renovation creates an excellent opening for home performance work, because the walls are already coming apart. An infrared camera or a professional home energy audit is a good way to learn where your home is losing energy before you close anything back up.

Replace any soiled or ineffective insulation, seal gaps and cracks, and consider replacing leaky or single-pane windows. Whenever possible, choose insulation products that contain natural materials, do not contain harmful flame retardants, and do not off-gas VOCs.

You’ll need to budget for this work differently than you would have in 2024. The 25C Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit, which returned up to $3,200 a year on insulation, windows, heat pumps, and energy audits, was terminated for property placed in service after December 31, 2025, under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The 25D residential clean energy credit ended on the same date. What survived is the Inflation Reduction Act’s Home Energy Rebates that provide up to $8,000 for whole-home efficiency retrofits and up to $14,000 for electrification. The program is administered state by state and generally limited to households with incomes below 150 percent of local median income.

These rebates, which can be exhausted during the year, are first-come, first-served, so availability is uneven. California’s single-family electrification rebates were fully reserved by February 2026 and moved to a waitlist; Colorado is running staged regional rounds; Oregon launched in spring 2026; Texas and Tennessee had not opened to applicants as of mid-2026.

Start with your research with the state energy office, confirm whether pre-approval is required before you buy equipment, and stack utility rebates on top. Several states disqualify projects that were purchased before the paperwork went in.

Conserve Water

Do your sinks have water-saving fittings, and are your showerheads efficient? A standard showerhead uses 2.5 gallons per minute; a WaterSense labeled model uses no more than 2.0 gpm and must pass spray force and coverage testing to earn the label. The EPA calculates the average family can save 2,700 gallons of water and more than 330 kilowatt-hours of water heating energy per year with the swap.

A renovation is also the right moment to chase down leaks. Household leaks waste roughly 180 gallons a week, and a running toilet flapper or a dripping supply line is far easier to find and fix while a plumber is already on site.

These steps, and many more, can turn your home improvement project into an environmental improvement outcome.

Editor’s Note: This article was originally published on October 30, 2019, and was most recently updated in July 2026.

articles.personality_title: Nine practical tips to make home renovations greener and more efficient
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Renovating a home is a good time to improve how it works and looks. It also creates a lot of waste. In 2018, the U.S. made 600 million tons of debris from building work, with most of it going to landfills.

**What happened** – Experts shared nine tips to help people reduce waste, save water and energy, and use recycled or eco-friendly materials during home renovation projects. These include reusing old cabinets and fixtures, donating leftover materials, replacing old toilets and appliances with efficient ones, and choosing products with low harmful chemicals. They also explained new rules and rebates that help pay for energy-saving upgrades.

**Impact** – These tips can lower the amount of trash sent to landfills and reduce water and electricity use in homes. For example, replacing old toilets can save thousands of gallons of water each year. Using recycled materials adds character to homes and keeps useful items out of the trash. The advice helps homeowners make smarter choices that benefit both their homes and the environment.

**What's next step** – Homeowners should plan their renovations with these green ideas in mind. They can check local programs for rebates on energy upgrades and find places to donate or buy recycled materials. Contractors and DIY renovators can also use this guide to reduce waste and improve home comfort.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Simple changes during home renovations, like reusing materials and upgrading to efficient appliances, can save resources and reduce waste while improving your home.

Arielle:

But that is actually a sign that, uh, your plant is stressed out. The plant is redirecting energy towards reproduction because it’s struggling to survive. The article goes through a bunch of tips that you can use, uh, before watering anything, like sticking your finger in the top inch or two of soil, see if it’s wet, because if it is wet, then more water will likely make things worse.

So overwatering, underwatering, compacted soil, and root rot can all look the same from the outside, and the soil check helps narrow down what the actual problem is. Prevention does beat rescue. General guidelines to follow, uh, are to water deeply in the early morning and direct it to the soil around the roots, not onto leaves or stems.

And it’s important to note that even full sun plants can benefit from temporary shade on extreme heat days, and we’re getting a lot more of extreme heat days, uh, now. So a shade cloth or even old bed sheets draped over them during peak afternoon hours can help them out. The next article had a very surprising title to me.

It’s called “The Newcastle researcher turning ocean plastic into a dolphin rescue strategy”. Ocean plastic is usually the villain in marine wildlife stories, and for good reason. But this one is different. A researcher at Newcastle University is attaching empty plastic bottles to fishing nets, and it’s actually helping dolphins survive them.

The mechanism is pretty weird, pretty fascinating. Just to explain how this works, there are gill nets that hang vertically in the water, and they are nearly invisible to dolphin echolocation. Um, the nylon is too sparse and acoustically too similar to water to produce a return signal, so dolphins won’t detect any danger and will swim into them.

And of course, that, that injures them, or worst case scenario, will even kill them. Current numbers say that around 1,000 porpoises and hundreds of dolphins, including 250 common dolphins, die in UK gill nets every year alone. Professor Per Berggren at Newcastle University asked the question, what if you gave the net something that does produce an echo?

Plastic bottles are what he decided to use. The air inside reflects echolocation clicks, giving dolphins a strong return signal that they can read and respond to. And then there’s also glass bottles, uh, with metal bolts inside that create a clinking sound as they move in the water, and that passive noise cue works alongside or instead of echolocation.

There have been a few trials across 1,600 nets in Zanzibar, Peru, and Brazil, and the study or the results were published in Fisheries Research and Marine Mammal Science. There were a lot of really positive results, but the Peru results were mixed, and for nets set near the surface, bottles didn’t reduce dolphin bycatch, but did increase target fish catch.

So yeah, it also increased shark bycatch. So I guess this is still being studied and developed as a solution. But overall, it seems that attaching plastic bottles can rescue dolphin bycatch globally. And honestly, it’s a solution that every fisher can afford to do.

Karissa:

Hmm. Yeah, that’s the important part here is that, you know, it’s a low-cost solution, and it’s more accessible than these, you know, really fancy, expensive technologies that not, not all fishers can afford.

Arielle:

Yeah, I think it’s particularly optimistic to know that the source of the problem can also be part of the solution. Um, and in case you’re wondering, no plastic bottles were lost during the trial, so it, this study did not contribute more to ocean plastic. The next solution is titled: “What India’s hydrogen train launch means for its vast railway network”.

So India just launched a hydrogen-powered train, and the interesting part isn’t just that it runs on hydrogen, it’s that it was built locally. It was built in India. This is a country of 1.4 billion people with one of the world’s largest rail networks, and this is the first step toward cleaning up the diesel routes.

So this domestically built hydrogen-powered train launched in July, um, I think it was the 18th of July. Um, and it was named the Namo Green Rail, which Namo is a common abbreviation of the Prime Minister Modi’s name, so his name is Narendra Modi, Namo. Um, just for people who are unfamiliar, hydrogen fuel cells combine hydrogen and oxygen to generate electricity, and the only direct emission is water vapor.

This pilot train also includes hydrogen storage and refueling infrastructure, and they’re kind of testing the whole system, not just the train itself. India’s net zero target is 2070, and this is part of a national push to develop green hydrogen domestically and cut transport emissions. Several other countries have already developed hydrogen trains, um, but India’s version stands out because it was built in country.

Karissa:

The self-reliant India here shows that it’s not just a clean energy story, it’s an industrial capability story of India and other countries being able to produce this inside their own countries.

Arielle:

The next solution is more of a lifestyle one, and it kind of links to a solution that we talked about last week, Karissa.

It’s titled: “The case for clearing your calendar one weekend a month”. Most of us have spent the summer going to things we were excited about basically all summer, and now it might feel like we’re just getting through it. This story is about the empty weekend or, like, the one weekend a month with nothing on the calendar, and why it might be the most restorative thing you can do for the rest of the summer.

Now, last week, Karissa and I were talking about why summer days feel like they’re going so fast and why the summer season feels like it just disappears, and part of that reason is because we’re not taking enough time just to relax and enjoy and kind of do nothing but appreciate what’s right in front of you.

So this article is kind of a complement to that, and it goes deeper into this, um, one empty weekend a month idea, which started with parents who were done with the nonstop churn of kids’ weekend activities. And then in response to that, they canceled everything and had some of the best days they’d had in months.

I don’t know about you, Karissa, but I’m guilty of filling my weekends by reflex. So it just feels like I should be doing something, and an open Saturday can feel almost suspicious, like you must be forgetting something that you scheduled. Hmm. Or, like, you feel the guilt, the sunshine guilt of, like, needing to do something with the good weather.

Karissa:

I feel like I’m definitely guilty of that as well. I mean, it’s kind of this big trap of treating an empty weekend like it can just be a productive weekend instead. And so it’s important to resist, you know, the urge to tackle some home projects and stuff, so.

Arielle:

Yeah, you make a good point, that even when you do have a weekend day with nothing planned, you end up being, like, quote, unquote, productive

’cause you feel like you have to do something with it. So yeah, I, I feel like I would struggle with this, but I am gonna try and have, like, one weekend for the rest of the summer. I mean, it’s August, so- … I only have basically one more month to do this. Um- I know. Me too … but I’m gonna try to just have that one weekend where I don’t do anything.

Um-

Karissa:

Yeah, exactly. And of course, the solution extends past summer as well. It’s, uh, good to keep in mind just year-round that it’s okay to take a weekend to actually just rest and restore.

Arielle:

The last solution that I’m going to share this week is called “Oakland kids can now borrow sports gear for free at this special library”.

Youth sports in the US now cost the average family over 1,000 a year per child, and that number is still climbing. A park supervisor in East Oakland had a little budget left at the end of the year and an idea. This is the story of the sports equipment lending library she built for a neighborhood that’s been making do without enough for a long time.

As I mentioned, youth sports cost the average US family $1,016 a year per child, and that’s up 46% since 2019. And in Oakland, just 14% of kids get the recommended 60 minutes of daily physical activity, compared to the 23% nationally. So this Park Play Lending Library opened early in July, July 11th, at the Larry E. Reid Sports Center in Brookfield Village, East Oakland, in case you’re familiar with the area. And there you can check out a soccer ball, a football, volleyball, yoga mat, or tennis equipment, and then take it to the park, have your fun, and bring it right back. There’s actually also board games, too, because the community asked for that, so those are now available.

And basically the goal is anything that gets people outside and moving.

Karissa:

Mm-hmm.

Arielle:

This idea, it’s based on Oakland and Berkeley’s long-running Tool Lending Libraries. So it’s just the same logic applied to sports.

Karissa:

This is a pilot, but if it holds, the plan is adding one lending library per Oakland district, stocked based on what each community requests.

And also, um, they wanna partner with local sports organizations so they can make this equipment more accessible to more people. And this is a model that’s easily able to be replicated in other communities, so I think it’s very interesting. And yeah, I mean, sports are very expensive. I remember as a child, um, when I was in youth sports, like I did cheerleading, for instance, and every year that’s like a $500 bill for my parents, and that was like 20 years ago.

But I mean, it’s even more now. It was expensive having to get all the uniforms and the stuff we needed, and pay for, like, the coaches and stuff. So it’s really expensive and can be unaccessible for a lot of people.

Arielle:

Yeah, and that’s just not fair because there’s so many benefits to playing team sports.

I wouldn’t really know them ’cause I didn’t do that. I was so not coordinated as a kid, and, like, very shy and insecure about joining anything team-related. Um-

Karissa:

Mm-hmm …

Arielle:

but my sisters played sports, and they still do, and I know that they gained a lot of, uh, you know, leadership and teamwork, and all- Yeah … of these things that can help you later on in your life.

So if money is the barrier, then we should do everything we can to tear that barrier down.

Karissa:

Mm-hmm. Absolutely.

Arielle:

Those were all the solutions that we had on The Optimist Daily this week, but we do have an Emissary shout-out from Marc and Lena-Maria.

Karissa:

Yeah. Thank you, Marc and Lena-Maria, for supporting The Optimist Daily.

They wanted to shout out James Arbib and Tony Seba’s RethinkX. RethinkX is a fully independent, not-for-profit organization, and they produce impartial research on global technology disruptions to accurately predict system change and guide humanity to an age of super abundance and freedom. So a really cool nonprofit that is investigating all these technologies.

Arielle:

Mm-hmm. And emphasis on impartial. We really need that, um, objective kind of look at things. So yeah, this seems really great. We are going to link it in the show notes as always. And once again, a huge thank you to Marc and Lena-Maria for being a part of this, um, solutions-minded mission that we are trying to encourage the world to come along with us on.

If you are an Emissary and you want to send a shout-out over to us, like Marc and Lena-Maria did, then that link should be in your inbox somewhere. Um, but Karissa and I will send it out again sometime soon, or you can email us at podcast@optimistdaily.com to find that link again. And we’ll just send it to you directly.

If you’re not an Emissary yet and you want to be, again, you can find out how to do that in the show notes.

Karissa:

Well, before we sign off for this time, we have a positive quote to share with you.

Arielle:

So this is from Cora Coralina, and she was a Brazilian writer and poet. “Recreate your life, always. Remove the stones.

Plant rose bushes and make sweets. Begin again.”

Karissa:

I love that one. There’s always time to recreate your life, so.

Arielle:

Hmm. It’s never too late to restart. Well, Karissa, I hope you enjoy your trip.

Karissa:

Yeah. And I hope you enjoy your trip as well, Arielle. It’ll be a great time to refresh, restore, and adventure a bit.

In Florida, planting milkweed along roadsides creates safe migration paths for monarch butterflies.

Liquid air batteries can store energy for days, helping provide power even when the sun or wind is absent. Roadside milkweed supports monarch butterflies and other pollinators in areas where natural habitats are shrinking.

articles.content:
New-ish monkeys: This pair of colobus monkeys (Colobus congoensis) belong to a new species discovered by scientists in the forests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). However, local people have known about the species for decades, calling them “Likweli” or “kasaba nkoni”. The monkeys are shy and elusive, hiding in the canopy of the forest between the Lomami and Lilo rivers in the DRC. They have distinctive orange lips, which flare out when they make sounds called roars, which are punctuated by short snorts. Conservationists first spotted the unidentified monkeys in 2008, but a second sighting in 2018 led to a dedicated expedition to document them. The findings of the expedition were published this month in PLOS One.

Credit: Daniel Rosengren/Frankfurt Zoological Society

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it adds to what we know about animals in the DRC and helps protect this unique species. It also shows how local knowledge can guide scientific research. Finding new animals like this helps conservation groups work to keep forests and wildlife safe.

articles.title: How Europe can make its landscapes more fire-resilient
articles.summary: Paradoxically, suppressing wildfires has also made European countries more vulnerable to huge blazes like those seen in France and Spain this week. With global warming also amplifying the danger, some experts are calling for a change of strategy
articles.content:
Paradoxically, suppressing wildfires has also made European countries more vulnerable to huge blazes like those seen in France and Spain this week. With global warming also amplifying the danger, some experts are calling for a change of strategy

Firefighters battle a wildfire in Cebreros, Spain Cesar MANSO/AFP via Getty Images

As unprecedented wildfires continue to burn in France and Spain, the blame game has also heated up. Right-wing opposition politicians have claimed both governments under-invested in water bombers because nearly half of their Canadair planes are out of operation. Officials have accused conservative-led regions like Madrid, where the forest fire service is only half-staffed, of undermining fire control.

But experts say the debates over firefighting are focusing on the symptoms rather than the disease. Instead, Europe must invest more in fire prevention such as prescribed burns, and even allow some wildfires to burn. That includes the UK, where a wildfire in Suffolk came within 5 kilometres of the Sizewell nuclear power station and another burned 25 square kilometres of moorland and forest in the Cairngorms, Scotland.

“You can double the number of planes; you can triple it. It will be very, very costly, and every single euro you put there is not a euro that is invested in prevention,” says Sebastien Lahaye at the French wildfire consultancy Warucene. “You will nevertheless have one fire or several fires that will escape and that will become this huge fire.”

Advertisement

The ingredients of a catastrophic wildfire are drought, heat and an accumulation of fuel, and this year has mixed in a generous portion of all three. A wet spring in parts of Europe increased vegetation, which then dried out in a widespread drought this summer. Now much of the continent is suffering through its fourth heatwave.

More than 4300 square kilometres have gone up in flames across the European Union, a pace that, if it continues, will break the record of 10,800 square kilometres burned last year. Record-sized wildfires near Bordeaux and Madrid forced one of the largest evacuations since the second world war.

Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter

In southern Europe, the average number of wildfires each year and the area burned has actually declined since 1981, according to a study this week by Raúl Cordero at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands and his colleagues. Mediterranean countries have warned the public against campfires and cigarettes in woodlands and got better at quickly extinguishing blazes by training firefighters and buying planes and helicopters.

But this crackdown has created a tinderbox. Shrubs and brush have proliferated, so those fires that do get out of hand are more likely to blow up into extreme megafires. This “suppression paradox” has been compounded by an exodus of people from rural areas to cities, leaving former farms and pastures overgrown. At the same time, more houses have sprung up in forests outside cities like Barcelona, raising the risk of wildfires, which most often are ignited by humans.

Now global warming is catching up with the improvements in wildfire suppression. Hot, dry and windy fire weather days have more than doubled across much of southern Europe, the study found.

“What’s occurring this year seemed to confirm our hypothesis… that we are about to enter a new era of large fires that didn’t exist in Europe because of the successful fire suppression and education,” says Cordero.

Rather than responding with more suppression, Europe must embrace the often uncomfortable task of making landscapes fire-resilient. Roughly speaking, 90 per cent of the fire budget in many countries goes towards fighting fires and 10 per cent towards preventing them, according Johann Goldammer at the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry in Germany.

“It should be the other way round, to invest 90 per cent of whatever is financially available in prevention and proactive measures, so that in the end, only 10 per cent would be needed for suppression,” he says.

The EU has been working to restore nature in 20 per cent of its land area by 2030 to combat the climate and biodiversity crises. But in many cases, woodlands need to be more intensively managed, including through sustainable logging, Goldammer argues.

Logging alone is not enough. The fire near Bordeaux raged through Europe’s largest human-made forest in Landes, 10,000 square kilometres of land that was once so swampy that shepherds walked on stilts. Napoleon III reclaimed the marshes by planting maritime pines, which are still harvested for paper and lumber.

Especially since a devastating 2022 fire there, landowners have built access roads, water ditches and fire breaks. But they also replanted the pine monoculture, a practice that raises fire risk. Similar monocultures of eucalyptus in Portugal have fuelled blazes like the Pedrógão Grande fire, which killed 66 people in 2017. While diversifying trees in the Landes may be difficult, the fire breaks at least need to be widened and increased, says Lahaye.

Even where forests don’t have fire breaks cleared to the bare ground, trees can be thinned and brush cleared to create fuel breaks. Re-establishing orchards, vineyards, pastures and agriculture can help create a “mosaic” of higher and lower fire fuel loads, rather than the uninterrupted tree cover that allowed the Bordeaux and Madrid fires to explode out of control.

Spanish regions have deployed herds of goats, sheep and cows to devour flammable brush. But in France, only 30 per cent of risky brush has been cleared due to conflicts between wildfire regulations and biodiversity regulations.

The most effective way to clear undergrowth is often through prescribed burns. Wildfires in the western US in 2020 were 16 per cent less severe in areas that had previously undergone prescribed burns, and they emitted 14 per cent less harmful particulate pollution as well.

But Europe is much more densely populated, and locals often see the technique as a threat. In some areas, regulations still often prevent it. While prescribed burning has been conducted along roads in the Landes, it is excluded from the timber plantations.

Sometimes it’s best not to fight wildfires at all, especially in winter, says Stefan Doerr at Swansea University, UK, although this is even more controversial.

“Firefighters from near Barcelona, they would tell you if there’s a fire in a forest and there are not particularly strong winds, let it burn because it will then not burn again for a long time under windier conditions,” says Doerr. “Everybody likes a nice pine forest… but it’s a bomb.”

articles.personality_title_es: Europa apuesta por una mejor prevención de incendios para proteger sus paisajes
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Europa ha enfrentado incendios grandes recientemente, especialmente en Francia y España. Estos incendios se han empeorado por el clima seco, el calor y el aumento de plantas que se queman fácilmente. Durante años, los países se concentraron en apagar los fuegos rápidamente, pero ahora los expertos dicen que esta forma ha empeorado el problema.

**Qué pasó** – Los expertos piden un nuevo método para manejar los incendios. En lugar de solo apagar los fuegos cuando empiezan, sugieren gastar más dinero en prevenirlos antes de que crezcan. Esto incluye quemas controladas, donde se prenden pequeños fuegos a propósito para limpiar plantas secas, y mejor manejo de los bosques como aclarar árboles y limpiar maleza. Algunos lugares en Europa ya están probando estas ideas.

**Impacto** – Este cambio es importante porque ayuda a reducir el riesgo de incendios grandes y peligrosos que pueden destruir hogares, bosques y animales. Por ejemplo, dejar que pequeños fuegos ardan o usar animales como cabras para comer la maleza puede evitar que los incendios se extiendan. Esta nueva estrategia también ahorra dinero porque se necesita menos lucha contra incendios grandes.

**Qué sigue** – Los países europeos y la Unión Europea planean invertir más en prevención de incendios y cuidado del paisaje. Esto puede significar cambiar leyes para permitir más quemas controladas y manejar los bosques de manera diferente. Las comunidades cerca de los bosques también aprenderán a vivir con seguridad con el riesgo de incendios.

**Una frase clave** – Europa está cambiando de solo apagar incendios a prevenirlos con un mejor cuidado forestal y quemas controladas para proteger mejor a las personas y la naturaleza.
